propositions.text: The Court considers the statutory regime governing bail pending appeal in the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: This appeal provides the Court with an opportunity to consider and clarify the statutory regime in the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , which governs bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Focus on principles guiding appellate courts on bail for convicted persons pending appeal.
propositions.quote: In particular, we are concerned with the principles and policy considerations by which appellate courts should be guided in deciding whether a person, like the appellant Dennis James Oland, who has been convicted of a serious crime and sentenced to a lengthy term of imprisonment, should be released on bail pending the determination of his appeal against conviction.

paragraphs.summary: The Court considers the Criminal Code's bail pending appeal regime and principles guiding appellate courts on bail for convicted persons pending appeal.

propositions.text: The appeal focuses on interpretation and application of ss. 679(3) and 680(1) of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: The debate in this appeal focuses on the interpretation and application of two relatively brief provisions of the Code — s. 679(3) and s. 680(1) .

propositions.text: Section 679(3) allows release pending appeal if appellant shows appeal is not frivolous, will surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
propositions.quote: 679 . . . (3) In the case of an appeal [against conviction], the judge of the court of appeal may order that the appellant be released pending the determination of his appeal if the appellant establishes that (a) the appeal . . . is not frivolous; (b) he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order; and (c) his detention is not necessary in the public interest.

propositions.text: Section 680(1) allows review of a judge's bail decision by the court of appeal, which may vary or substitute the decision.
propositions.quote: 680 (1) A decision made by a judge under section . . . 679 may, on the direction of the chief justice or acting chief justice of the court of appeal, be reviewed by that court and that court may, if it does not confirm the decision, (a) vary the decision; or (b) substitute such other decision as, in its opinion, should have been made.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal focuses on ss. 679(3) and 680(1) of the Criminal Code, which set criteria and review for bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland applied for bail pending appeal after second degree murder conviction; application denied under public interest criterion.
propositions.quote: In the present case, Mr. Oland applied for bail pending appeal following his conviction on a charge of second degree murder involving the death of his father. His application was denied under the public interest criterion set out in s. 679(3) (c).

propositions.text: Public safety was not an issue; appeal judge found public confidence in justice would not be maintained if released.
propositions.quote: While public safety was not in issue, the appeal judge was not persuaded that public confidence in the administration of justice would be maintained if Mr. Oland were to be released.

propositions.text: Review panel found appeal judge's detention decision neither unreasonable nor based on material error.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the three-judge review panel, the decision of the appeal judge to detain Mr. Oland was “neither unreasonable nor the product of any material error of fact, law or mixed law and fact” (2016 NBCA 15, 446 N.B.R. (2d) 325, at para. 15).

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker denied Mr. Oland bail pending appeal under public interest; review panel upheld that decision as reasonable.

propositions.text: Detaining Mr. Oland on public interest grounds was clearly unwarranted in the circumstances.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am respectfully of the view that detaining Mr. Oland on the public interest criterion was clearly unwarranted in the circumstances.

propositions.text: Appeal judge made a material legal error affecting the outcome.
propositions.quote: Moreover, in his reasons, the learned appeal judge made a material legal error that affected the outcome.

propositions.text: Review panel erred in failing to intervene on the detention order.
propositions.quote: It follows, in my respectful view, that the review panel erred in failing to intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds detaining Mr. Oland was unwarranted, the appeal judge erred legally, and the review panel erred by not intervening.

propositions.text: Before this Court's hearing, New Brunswick Court of Appeal allowed Mr. Oland's appeal and ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: As it turns out, prior to Mr. Oland’s appeal being argued in this Court, the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick heard and allowed his appeal from conviction and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was released on bail pending re-trial.
propositions.quote: In consequence, Mr. Oland was released on bail pending his re-trial.

propositions.text: This Court's appeal was rendered moot but was heard on merits and allowed with no further order.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, his appeal to this Court from the order of the review panel upholding his detention order was rendered moot. However, for reasons which I will explain, we chose to hear the appeal on its merits — and having done so, we would allow the appeal but make no further order.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes the appeal became moot after a new trial was ordered and bail granted, but hears and allows the appeal with no further order.

propositions.text: Richard Oland was found bludgeoned to death on July 7, 2011; Mr. Oland became primary suspect and was charged with second degree murder.
propositions.quote: On July 7, 2011, Mr. Oland’s father, Richard Oland, was found bludgeoned to death at his office in Saint John, New Brunswick. During the ensuing police investigation, Mr. Oland became the primary suspect. He was eventually arrested and charged with second degree murder on November 12, 2013.

paragraphs.summary: Richard Oland was murdered in 2011; Mr. Oland was charged with second degree murder in 2013.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was released on bail pending trial in 2013; convicted of second degree murder in 2015; sentenced to life imprisonment with no parole for 10 years in 2016.
propositions.quote: On November 18, 2013, following a contested hearing, Mr. Oland was released on bail pending trial upon entering into a surety recognizance in the amount of $50,000, with conditions. On December 19, 2015, after a three-month trial by judge and jury, he was convicted of second degree murder. On February 11, 2016, the trial judge sentenced him to life imprisonment with no chance of parole for 10 years.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland was released on bail pending trial, convicted in 2015, and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2016.

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Oland was well-educated, devoted family man without criminal past, posing no realistic future danger.
propositions.quote: In his sentencing reasons, the trial judge found that apart from the offence for which he now stood convicted, Mr. Oland was “a well-educated 47 year old husband and devoted father without a criminal past”, and “a loving/caring man; a man at the heart of his family and a contributing member of his community” (2016 NBQB 43, 447 N.B.R. (2d) 7, at paras. 14 and 18).

propositions.text: Trial judge found Mr. Oland posed no realistic risk of future dangerousness and had excellent reintegration prospects.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the trial judge, Mr. Oland posed no realistic risk of future dangerousness and his prospect of successfully reintegrating into society after serving his sentence was excellent.

propositions.text: The offence was brutal with about 40 injuries but was a spontaneous outburst from family dysfunction and stress, closer to manslaughter than first degree murder.
propositions.quote: As for the offence, the trial judge characterized it as “brutal”, noting approximately 40 blunt and sharp force injuries inflicted to the deceased’s head. On the other hand, the crime involved a spontaneous outburst that was the product of a long-standing dysfunctional family dynamic and immense stress. For this reason, the trial judge found that it fell at the “lower end” on the continuum of moral culpability for second degree murder, closer to manslaughter than to first degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Oland a devoted family man posing no future danger; the brutal offence was a spontaneous outburst closer to manslaughter.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland filed notice of appeal from conviction and applied for bail pending appeal under s. 679(3).
propositions.quote: On January 20, 2016, Mr. Oland filed a notice of appeal from conviction with the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick. He advanced numerous grounds of appeal relating to three principal areas: errors in the jury charge; errors in admitting certain evidence; and the reasonableness of the verdict. At the same time, he applied under s. 679(3) of the Code for bail pending the determination of his appeal.

propositions.text: The outcome of the bail application is the focus of this appeal.
propositions.quote: The outcome of that application is the focus of this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland appealed his conviction and applied for bail pending appeal; the bail application outcome is the appeal's focus.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland filed affidavits supporting bail application, including good character, sureties, and trial transcript excerpts.
propositions.quote: In support of his application, Mr. Oland filed numerous affidavits attesting to his good character, past compliance with release conditions, and his roots in the community. In addition, he filed affidavits from two family members who were prepared to act as sureties and risk substantial sums of money should he breach the terms of his release order. Finally, he submitted excerpts from the trial transcripts pertinent to his grounds of appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland supported his bail application with affidavits on character, sureties, and trial transcript excerpts.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Mr. Oland met criteria that appeal was not frivolous and he would surrender.
propositions.quote: In ruling on the application, the appeal judge found that Mr. Oland had discharged his onus on the first two criteria for release under s. 679(3)(a) and (b) of the Code, namely: his appeal was not frivolous and he would surrender into custody as required.

propositions.text: Appeal judge divided public interest criterion into public safety and public confidence in justice.
propositions.quote: The appeal judge then considered the public interest criterion under s. 679(3) (c), dividing it into two parts — public safety and public confidence in the administration of justice.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge found Mr. Oland met the first two bail criteria and considered public interest as public safety and public confidence.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found Mr. Oland posed no danger to the public, adopting sentencing judge's findings.
propositions.quote: Commencing with public safety, the appeal judge was satisfied that Mr. Oland posed “no danger to the public at large” (para. 15). In this regard, he adopted the findings of the sentencing judge that Mr. Oland was a man of prior good behaviour, without criminal record, and that the offence was largely the product of unique relational and situation-specific difficulties existing between him and his father.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge found Mr. Oland posed no public danger, adopting the sentencing judge's findings.

propositions.text: Appeal judge found gravity and brutality of offence weighed in favour of detention under public confidence.
propositions.quote: Turning to public confidence, the appeal judge found that the gravity and brutality of the offence weighed in favour of Mr. Oland’s detention.

propositions.text: Grounds of appeal were arguable but not strong enough to virtually assure new trial or acquittal.
propositions.quote: And while the grounds of appeal put forward by him were “clearly arguable”, they were not of such unique strength as to “virtually assure a new trial or an acquittal” (paras. 30 and 32).

propositions.text: Appeal judge was not persuaded public confidence would be maintained if Mr. Oland were released; bail denied.
propositions.quote: On balance, the appeal judge was not persuaded that public confidence in the administration of justice would be maintained if Mr. Oland were to be released. Accordingly, he dismissed the application for release pending appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge found the offence's gravity favored detention and denied bail for public confidence reasons.

propositions.text: Chief Justice directed a review of the detention order before a three-judge panel under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: On application by Mr. Oland under s. 680(1) of the Code, the Chief Justice of New Brunswick directed a review of his detention order before a three-judge panel of the court.

paragraphs.summary: The Chief Justice directed a review of Mr. Oland's detention order by a three-judge panel.

propositions.text: Review panel adopted deferential approach, viewing detention decision as a judgment call.
propositions.quote: In arriving at its decision, the panel adopted a deferential approach to the review, characterizing the appeal judge’s decision to detain Mr. Oland as a “judgment call”.

propositions.text: Panel recognized grounds of appeal were serious but noted conviction for brutal murder with mandatory life sentence.
propositions.quote: While the panel recognized that the grounds of appeal put forward by Mr. Oland were “serious”, he nonetheless stood convicted of a brutal murder for which he had received a mandatory life sentence.

propositions.text: Denying bail would not render appeal pointless; no error found in appeal judge's reasons; detention not clearly unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In the circumstances, denying him bail would not render his appeal pointless. Of primary significance, Mr. Oland had failed to show any error in the reasons of the appeal judge that would warrant interference; nor had he persuaded the panel that his detention in the circumstances was clearly unreasonable.

propositions.text: Application for review was dismissed.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the application for review was dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The review panel deferred to the appeal judge, found no error, and dismissed the application for review of detention.

propositions.text: On October 24, 2016, New Brunswick Court of Appeal allowed Mr. Oland's appeal and ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: On October 24, 2016, the Court of Appeal of New Brunswick allowed Mr. Oland’s appeal from conviction and ordered a new trial.

propositions.text: On October 25, 2016, Mr. Oland was granted bail pending re-trial.
propositions.quote: On October 25, 2016, he was granted bail pending his re-trial.

propositions.text: The parties were alerted to address mootness due to these events.
propositions.quote: In view of these events, the parties were alerted that they should be prepared to address the issue of mootness.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed Mr. Oland's appeal and bail pending re-trial, raising mootness issues for this appeal.

propositions.text: The Court raised mootness issue at hearing start; parties and interveners urged hearing on merits.
propositions.quote: At the commencement of the hearing, the Court raised the issue of mootness and we were urged by the parties and interveners to hear the appeal on its merits.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland submitted the decision is significant as he might face same situation after re-trial.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the respondent Crown submitted that this Court’s decision was potentially of significance to them, as Mr. Oland might find himself in the same situation following his re-trial.

propositions.text: The Crown also submitted the decision was significant for future similar situations.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the respondent Crown submitted that this Court’s decision was potentially of significance to them, as Mr. Oland might find himself in the same situation following his re-trial.

propositions.text: All submitted guidance was needed to resolve inconsistent appellate bail approaches across Canada.
propositions.quote: In addition, all concerned submitted that guidance was needed from this Court to resolve inconsistent approaches to bail taken by appellate courts across the country.

propositions.text: Bail pending appeal is temporary and evasive of appellate review, making this case appropriate to resolve conflicting jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: And as bail pending appeal was, by its temporary nature, evasive of appellate review, this was an appropriate case to resolve the conflicting jurisprudence: see Borowski v. Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342; R. v. McNeil, 2009 SCC 3, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 66, at para. 2.

paragraphs.summary: The Court raised mootness; parties urged hearing on merits for guidance on bail pending appeal due to inconsistent approaches.

propositions.text: The Court decided to hear the appeal on merits due to unanimous party position and Borowski criteria.
propositions.quote: In view of the unanimous position taken by the parties and interveners, and considering that the appeal meets the criteria established in Borowski, the Court determined that it would proceed to hear the appeal on its merits.

paragraphs.summary: The Court decided to hear the appeal on its merits given unanimous party support and Borowski criteria.

propositions.text: Section 679(3) sets three criteria for bail pending appeal: appeal not frivolous, surrender, and detention not necessary in public interest.
propositions.quote: The three statutory criteria for bail pending appeal are found in s. 679(3) of the Code: 679 . . . (3) In the case of an appeal [against conviction], the judge of the court of appeal may order that the appellant be released pending the determination of his appeal if the appellant establishes that (a) the appeal . . . is not frivolous; (b) he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the order; and (c) his detention is not necessary in the public interest.

propositions.text: Applicant bears burden to prove each criterion on balance of probabilities, citing cases.
propositions.quote: The applicant seeking bail bears the burden of establishing that each criterion is met on a balance of probabilities: R. v. Ponak, [1972] 4 W.W.R. 316 (B.C.C.A.), at pp. 317-18; R. v. Iyer, 2016 ABCA 407, at para. 7 (CanLII); R. v. D’Amico, 2016 QCCA 183, at para. 10 (CanLII); R. v. Gill, 2015 SKCA 96, 465 Sask. R. 253, at para. 14.

paragraphs.summary: Section 679(3) sets three bail criteria; applicant must prove each on balance of probabilities, citing authorities.

propositions.text: First criterion requires appeal judge to ensure grounds of appeal are not frivolous, a very low bar.
propositions.quote: The first criterion requires the appeal judge to examine the grounds of appeal with a view to ensuring that they are not “not frivolous” (s. 679(3)(a)). Courts have used different language to describe this standard. While not in issue on this appeal, the “not frivolous” test is widely recognized as being a very low bar: see R. v. Xanthoudakis, 2016 QCCA 1809, at paras. 4-7 (CanLII); R. v. Manasseri, 2013 ONCA 647, 312 C.C.C. (3d) 132, at para. 38; R. v. Passey, 1997 ABCA 343, 121 C.C.C. (3d) 444, at paras. 6-8; G. T. Trotter, The Law of Bail in Canada (3rd ed. (loose-leaf)), at pp. 10-13 to 10-15.

paragraphs.summary: The first bail criterion requires the appeal judge to ensure grounds are not frivolous, a very low standard.

propositions.text: Applicant must show he will surrender into custody per release order terms (s. 679(3)(b))
propositions.quote: The second criterion requires the applicant to show that “he will surrender himself into custody in accordance with the terms of the [release] order” (s. 679(3)(b)).

propositions.text: Appeal judge must be satisfied applicant will not flee and will surrender as required
propositions.quote: The appeal judge must be satisfied that the applicant will not flee the jurisdiction and will surrender into custody as required.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must show he will surrender into custody and not flee as required by s. 679(3)(b).

propositions.text: Applicant must establish detention not necessary in public interest (s. 679(3)(c))
propositions.quote: The third criterion requires the applicant to establish that “his detention is not necessary in the public interest” (s. 679(3)(c)).

propositions.text: Mr. Oland's bail pending appeal failed on public interest criterion
propositions.quote: It is upon this criterion that Mr. Oland’s bid for bail pending appeal failed

propositions.text: Parties seek guidance on how strength of grounds of appeal affects public interest detention analysis
propositions.quote: the parties ask this Court for guidance on how the strength of the grounds of appeal from a conviction should be considered in determining whether detention is necessary in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Mr. Oland failed bail on public interest grounds and parties seek guidance on considering appeal strength in that analysis.

propositions.text: Farinacci (1993) defined public interest criterion as public safety and public confidence components
propositions.quote: she determined that the public interest criterion consisted of two components: public safety and public confidence in the administration of justice (pp. 47-48).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Farinacci defining public interest as public safety and public confidence components.

propositions.text: Public safety relates to protection of public and tracks secondary ground for release pending trial
propositions.quote: She found that it related to the protection and safety of the public and essentially tracked the familiar requirements of the so-called “secondary ground” governing an accused’s release pending trial (pp. 45 and 47-48).

propositions.text: Public confidence involves weighing enforceability and reviewability interests
propositions.quote: The public confidence component, on the other hand, was more nuanced and required elaboration. It involved the weighing of two competing interests: enforceability and reviewability.

paragraphs.summary: Farinacci held public safety concerns public protection; public confidence weighs enforceability against reviewability interests.

propositions.text: Enforceability means respecting immediate enforceability of judgments
propositions.quote: the enforceability interest reflected the need to respect the general rule of the immediate enforceability of judgments.

propositions.text: Reviewability means society acknowledges justice system fallibility and need for meaningful appeal review
propositions.quote: Reviewability, on the other hand, reflected society’s acknowledgement that our justice system is not infallible and that persons who challenge the legality of their convictions should be entitled to a meaningful review process

paragraphs.summary: Farinacci explained enforceability as respecting immediate judgment enforcement; reviewability as society's recognition of justice system fallibility.

propositions.text: Farinacci framework has stood the test of time and is universally endorsed by appellate courts
propositions.quote: The public interest framework which it established has withstood the test of time. It has been universally endorsed by appellate courts across the country

propositions.text: All parties and interveners in this appeal accept Farinacci framework and none seek to revisit it
propositions.quote: all of the parties and interveners in this appeal are content with the Farinacci framework. None has spoken against it; none has asked us to revisit it

propositions.text: Court sees no reason to revisit Farinacci; it remains good law
propositions.quote: I see no reason to do so. Farinacci remains good law in my view.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci remains good law, universally endorsed, and all parties accept it without challenge.

propositions.text: Public safety and public confidence components are not separate silos; public safety concerns inform public confidence analysis
propositions.quote: where the public safety threshold has been met by an applicant seeking bail pending appeal, residual public safety concerns or the absence of any public safety concerns remain relevant and should be considered in the public confidence analysis.

propositions.text: Public safety alone can justify detention, but public safety and confidence components overlap
propositions.quote: there will be cases where public safety considerations alone are sufficient to warrant a detention order in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains public safety and confidence components overlap and public safety concerns inform public confidence analysis.

propositions.text: Difficulty arises in applying Farinacci to public confidence component balancing enforceability and reviewability
propositions.quote: Appellate judges continue to have difficulty resolving the tension between enforceability and reviewability, especially in cases like the present one

paragraphs.summary: The court notes appellate judges struggle to balance enforceability and reviewability under Farinacci's public confidence component.

propositions.text: Cases involving public confidence component in bail pending appeal are rare exceptions
propositions.quote: cases like this tend to be more the exception than the rule.

propositions.text: Appellate judges regularly handle bail pending appeal; public confidence rarely central
propositions.quote: Appellate judges across the country deal with applications for bail pending appeal on a regular basis. Of those, only a fraction are likely to involve the public confidence component.

propositions.text: Porisky: Not every offence is serious enough to engage public confidence assessment; Crown should exercise judgment
propositions.quote: Not every offence is serious enough to engage an assessment of the merits. There is no need to go beyond the frivolous threshold in cases unlikely to arouse a concern about public confidence. . . . [W]e should expect Crown counsel to recognize that the continuum runs from petty theft to first degree murder and to exercise good judgment in raising public confidence only in those cases where the offence is at the serious end of the scale.

paragraphs.summary: The court states public confidence issues in bail appeals are rare; Porisky advises Crown to raise public confidence only for serious offences.

propositions.text: Court proposes to elaborate on enforceability and reviewability interests to guide appellate judges
propositions.quote: I propose to elaborate somewhat on the competing interests of enforceability and reviewability identified in Farinacci.

paragraphs.summary: The court proposes elaborating on enforceability and reviewability interests to assist appellate judges.

propositions.text: Parliament provides no direction on public confidence in release pending appeal orders in s. 679(3)(c)
propositions.quote: In section 679(3)(c) of the Code, Parliament has not provided appellate judges with any direction as to how a release pending appeal order is likely to affect public confidence

propositions.text: Parliament identifies four factors in s. 515(10)(c) for bail pending trial public confidence
propositions.quote: Under s. 515(10)(c), Parliament has identified four factors that judges may consider in assessing whether a detention order is necessary to maintain public confidence

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) factors: strength of prosecution case, gravity of offence, circumstances including firearm use, potential lengthy imprisonment
propositions.quote: (i) the apparent strength of the prosecution’s case, (ii) the gravity of the offence, (iii) the circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence, including whether a firearm was used, and (iv) the fact that the accused is liable, on conviction, for a potentially lengthy term of imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 679(3)(c) lacks guidance but s. 515(10)(c) lists four bail pending trial public confidence factors.

propositions.text: Section 515(10)(c) factors, with modifications, should inform public confidence in release pending appeal
propositions.quote: these same factors — with appropriate modifications to reflect the post-conviction context — should be accounted for in considering how, if at all, a release pending appeal order is likely to affect public confidence

paragraphs.summary: The court argues s. 515(10)(c) factors should be adapted to assess public confidence in bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Using s. 515(10)(c) factors promotes consistency and fairness between trial and appellate bail contexts
propositions.quote: It has the virtue of promoting consistency and harmony between the trial and appellate contexts so that, together, they may be seen as providing a cohesive and comprehensive statement of the law governing bail in Canada.

propositions.text: Bail should not be more accessible post-conviction than pre-trial; this approach fosters fairness and confidence
propositions.quote: it accords with the basic principle that, in general, bail should not be more readily accessible for someone who has been convicted of a crime than for someone who is awaiting trial and is presumed innocent.

paragraphs.summary: The court argues adapting s. 515(10)(c) factors fosters consistency and fairness between pre-trial and post-conviction bail.

propositions.text: Presumption of innocence underlies greater bail accessibility pre-trial; s. 11(e) Charter protects reasonable bail
propositions.quote: Greater accessibility to bail pending trial is rooted in the presumption of innocence. Accused persons charged with an offence in Canada are presumed to be innocent... s. 11 (e) the right of every person charged with an offence “not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains pre-trial bail accessibility is rooted in presumption of innocence and s. 11(e) Charter rights.

propositions.text: Post-conviction, presumption of innocence is displaced and s. 11(e) Charter no longer applies
propositions.quote: once a conviction is entered, the presumption of innocence is displaced and s. 11 (e) of the Charter no longer applies.

propositions.text: Onus shifts to applicant for bail pending appeal; Crown no longer bears onus to detain
propositions.quote: for appeal purposes, Parliament has seen fit to reverse the onus onto the applicant in all cases.

paragraphs.summary: The court states post-conviction presumption of innocence ends and onus shifts to applicant for bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform public confidence component in s. 679(3)(c)
propositions.quote: I turn to the enforceability and reviewability interests to explain how... the public confidence factors listed in s. 515(10)(c) are instructive in identifying the factors that make up the public confidence component in s. 679(3)(c).

paragraphs.summary: The court will explain how s. 515(10)(c) factors inform the public confidence component in s. 679(3)(c).

propositions.text: Seriousness of crime is important in assessing public confidence for pre-trial detention and bail pending appeal
propositions.quote: In assessing whether public confidence concerns support a pre-trial detention order under s. 515(10)(c), the seriousness of the crime plays an important role... So too for bail pending appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court states seriousness of the crime is important in assessing public confidence for bail pending appeal.

propositions.text: Parliament's three factors for seriousness of crime in s. 515(10)(c) apply to s. 679(3)(c) with trial judge's sentencing reasons aiding appeal judge
propositions.quote: these factors are readily transferable to s. 679(3)(c) — the only difference being... the appeal judge will generally have the trial judge’s reasons for sentence

paragraphs.summary: The court holds s. 515(10)(c) seriousness factors apply to s. 679(3)(c) with trial judge's sentencing reasons aiding appeal judge.

propositions.text: Other factors like residual public safety or flight risks below substantial risk remain relevant under public confidence
propositions.quote: public safety concerns that fall short of the substantial risk mark... will remain relevant under the public confidence component and can... tip the scale in favour of detention

propositions.text: Absence of flight or public safety risks attenuates enforceability interest
propositions.quote: The same holds true for lingering flight risks that do not rise to the substantial risk level... By the same token, the absence of flight or public safety risks will attenuate the enforceability interest.

paragraphs.summary: The court states residual public safety or flight risks below substantial risk remain relevant; absence of such risks reduces enforceability interest.

propositions.text: Strength of prosecution's case under s. 515(10)(c)(i) translates to strength of grounds of appeal in appellate context
propositions.quote: The remaining factor... is the strength of the prosecution’s case... In the appellate context, this translates into the strength of the grounds of appeal

propositions.text: Strength of appeal plays central role in assessing reviewability interest despite concerns about merits assessment beyond s. 679(3)(a)
propositions.quote: in assessing the reviewability interest, the strength of an appeal plays a central role... some authorities have expressed concerns about assessing the merits of an appeal beyond the s. 679(3)(a) “not frivolous” criterion

paragraphs.summary: The court holds strength of grounds of appeal is central to reviewability interest despite some concerns about merits assessment.

propositions.text: The 'not frivolous' criterion in s. 679(3)(a) is an initial hurdle producing a categorical yes or no answer.
propositions.quote: the “not frivolous” criterion operates as an initial hurdle that produces a categorical “yes” or “no” answer, allowing for the immediate rejection of a release order in the face of a baseless appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 'not frivolous' criterion is an initial hurdle allowing immediate rejection of baseless appeals.

propositions.text: Justice Donald in Porisky said 'not frivolous' and 'sufficient merit' do not foreclose merits consideration beyond threshold.
propositions.quote: The express mention of “not frivolous” in s. 679(3)(a) and “sufficient merit” in s. 679(4) (a) does not, in my view, foreclose consideration of the merits for a purpose other than a threshold test.

propositions.text: The court agrees with Justice Donald that merits can be considered beyond threshold for public interest limits.
propositions.quote: Once over the threshold, the applicant faces the question of the public interest, a phrase not defined in the legislation but which had to be given some limits if it was to survive constitutional scrutiny. That is what Farinacci did.

propositions.text: Farinacci set boundaries for public interest criterion using merits assessment beyond threshold test.
propositions.quote: In setting boundaries for the public interest criterion, in particular the public confidence element, Farinacci employed the merits assessment for a purpose different from the threshold test.

propositions.text: Considering merits as part of public confidence question is authorized and not redundant.
propositions.quote: So I see no redundancy; nor do I doubt our authority to consider the merits as part of the public confidence question.

propositions.text: See also R. v. Delisle for similar reasoning.
propositions.quote: See also: R. v. Delisle, 2012 QCCA 1250, at paras. 4 and 52 (CanLII).

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with Justice Donald and Farinacci that merits can be considered beyond threshold for public interest limits.

propositions.text: Gary T. Trotter explained serious offences require probing inquiry into appeal chances beyond 'not frivolous' threshold.
propositions.quote: when an offence is serious, as with murder cases, such that public concern about enforceability is ignited, there should be a more probing inquiry into the chances of success on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Trotter that serious offences require more probing inquiry into appeal chances beyond threshold.

propositions.text: Appellate judges assess grounds of appeal for legal plausibility and record foundation to surpass 'not frivolous' standard.
propositions.quote: appellate judges will examine the grounds identified in the notice of appeal with an eye to their general legal plausibility and their foundation in the record.

propositions.text: Categories like 'prospect of success' are unhelpful and may complicate appeal strength assessment.
propositions.quote: Phrases such as “a prospect of success”, “a moderate prospect of success”, or “a realistic prospect of success” are generally not helpful.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellate judges assess appeal grounds for plausibility and avoid unhelpful categories like 'prospect of success'.

propositions.text: Appellate judges form preliminary assessments based on counsel materials and relevant authorities, not guesswork.
propositions.quote: appellate judges can be counted on to form their own “preliminary assessment” of the strength of an appeal based upon their knowledge and experience.

propositions.text: Review process is essential to maintain public confidence in justice administration beyond individual interests.
propositions.quote: a meaningful review process is essential to maintain public confidence in the administration of justice. Thus, there is a broader public interest in reviewability that transcends an individual’s interest in any given case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellate judges make informed preliminary assessments to maintain public confidence beyond individual interests.

propositions.text: Remedy sought on appeal may affect reviewability interest; lesser conviction reduces it even if grounds are strong.
propositions.quote: if a successful appeal can result only in a murder conviction being reduced to manslaughter, this will lessen the interest in reviewability, even if the grounds of appeal appear to be strong

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting that remedy affects reviewability interest.
propositions.quote: R. v. Meda (1981), 23 C.R. (3d) 174 (B.C.C.A.); R. v. Olsen (1996), 94 O.A.C. 62, at para. 5; R. v. Roe, 2008 BCCA 253, 256 B.C.A.C. 308, at para. 14; R. v. Lees, 1999 BCCA 441, 127 B.C.A.C. 280, at paras. 4-5.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the remedy sought on appeal may lessen reviewability interest, citing supporting cases.

propositions.text: Appellate judges must evaluate public confidence factors through eyes of reasonable, informed, dispassionate public member.
propositions.quote: public confidence is to be measured through the eyes of a reasonable member of the public. This person is someone who is thoughtful, dispassionate, informed of the circumstances of the case and respectful of society’s fundamental values

propositions.text: Cites R. v. St-Cloud for public confidence standard.
propositions.quote: R. v. St-Cloud, 2015 SCC 27, [2015] 2 S.C.R. 328, at paras. 74-80.

propositions.text: Public confidence must be distinguished from uninformed public opinion, which has no role in bail decisions.
propositions.quote: public confidence in the administration of justice must be distinguished from uninformed public opinion about the case, which has no role to play in the decision to grant bail or not.

paragraphs.summary: The court states public confidence is judged by a reasonable informed public, not uninformed opinion, citing St-Cloud.

propositions.text: Appellate judges should consider sentence length and appeal delay when balancing enforceability and reviewability.
propositions.quote: appellate judges should also be mindful of the anticipated delay in deciding an appeal, relative to the length of the sentence

propositions.text: Cites R. v. Baltovich for balancing sentence length and appeal delay.
propositions.quote: R. v. Baltovich (2000), 47 O.R. (3d) 761 (C.A.), at paras. 41-42.

propositions.text: If bail is impossible and sentence will mostly be served before appeal, consider expediting appeal under s. 679(10).
propositions.quote: where a bail order is out of the question, appellate judges should consider ordering the appeal expedited under s. 679(10) of the Code.

propositions.text: Expedited appeal preserves reviewability interest to some extent despite imperfections.
propositions.quote: While this may not be a perfect solution, it provides a means of preserving the reviewability interest at least to some extent.

paragraphs.summary: The court advises balancing sentence length and appeal delay, and expediting appeals if bail is impossible to preserve reviewability.

propositions.text: No precise formula exists to balance enforceability and reviewability; qualitative contextual assessment is required.
propositions.quote: there is no precise formula that can be applied to resolve the balance between enforceability and reviewability. A qualitative and contextual assessment is required.

propositions.text: Rejects categorical approach to murder or serious offences; principles apply uniformly.
propositions.quote: I would reject a categorical approach to murder or other serious offences, as proposed by certain interveners. Instead, the principles that I have discussed should be applied uniformly.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects categorical approaches and requires qualitative, contextual balancing of enforceability and reviewability.

propositions.text: Public interest in enforceability is high for murder or serious crimes and often outweighs reviewability, especially with safety or flight concerns or weak grounds.
propositions.quote: where the applicant has been convicted of murder or some other very serious crime, the public interest in enforceability will be high and will often outweigh the reviewability interest, particularly where there are lingering public safety or flight concerns and/or the grounds of appeal appear to be weak

propositions.text: Cites R. v. Mapara, Baltovich, Parsons for this principle.
propositions.quote: R. v. Mapara, 2001 BCCA 508, 158 C.C.C. (3d) 312, at para. 38; Baltovich, at para. 20; Parsons, at para. 44.

paragraphs.summary: The court states enforceability interest often outweighs reviewability for serious crimes with safety or flight concerns, citing cases.

propositions.text: If safety or flight concerns are negligible and grounds surpass 'not frivolous', reviewability may outweigh enforceability even for serious crimes.
propositions.quote: where public safety or flight concerns are negligible, and where the grounds of appeal clearly surpass the “not frivolous” criterion, the public interest in reviewability may well overshadow the enforceability interest, even in the case of murder or other very serious offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reviewability may outweigh enforceability if safety concerns are negligible and grounds surpass threshold, even for serious crimes.

propositions.text: Before applying principles, court will address principles governing review hearing under s. 680(1).
propositions.quote: Before applying these principles to the case at hand, I propose to address the principles that govern a review hearing under s. 680(1) of the Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court will address principles governing s. 680(1) review hearing before applying them to the case.

propositions.text: Section 680(1) reviews orders by single Court of Appeal judges under s. 679(3) and some pre-trial bail orders by superior court judges.
propositions.quote: s. 680(1) of the Code operates as a review mechanism for an order of a single judge of the Court of Appeal made under s. 679(3). I note, however, that the provision applies as well to certain pre-trial bail orders made by superior court judges for various offences, including murder.

propositions.text: Section 680(1) allows the court, on chief justice's direction, to review and vary or substitute decisions.
propositions.quote: 680 (1) A decision made by a judge under section 522 or subsection 524(4) or (5) or a decision made by a judge of the court of appeal under section 261 or 679 may, on the direction of the chief justice or acting chief justice of the court of appeal, be reviewed by that court and that court may, if it does not confirm the decision, (a) vary the decision; or (b) substitute such other decision as, in its opinion, should have been made.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 680(1) reviews single judge orders under s. 679(3) and allows court to vary or substitute decisions on chief justice's direction.

propositions.text: Review process has two stages: chief justice's initial vetting and court review if directed, usually by three judges.
propositions.quote: the review process consists of two stages: first, an initial vetting by the chief justice; and second, a review by the court, if directed by the chief justice. In practice, the review will generally be conducted by a panel of three judges, as it was in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 680(1) review involves chief justice vetting and panel review if directed, usually by three judges.

propositions.text: Chief justice's screening likely considers review nature and standard; panel's mandate should be addressed first.
propositions.quote: The nature of the review and the standard to be applied by the panel in deciding whether to interfere with the impugned order are factors that the chief justice is likely to take into account in carrying out his or her initial screening function. Accordingly, I find it useful to address the review panel’s mandate before addressing the chief justice’s screening function.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it useful to address the panel's mandate before the chief justice's screening function.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 680(1) panel review should apply correctness standard with robust independent review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the intervener Criminal Lawyers’ Association (Ontario) (“CLA”) submit that a standard of correctness should apply, meaning that the panel should engage in a robust review of the record and come to its own independent determination, irrespective of whether the single judge’s decision was tainted by legal error.

propositions.text: Respondent Crown and Attorneys General argue for deferential standard requiring legal error before intervention.
propositions.quote: The respondent Crown and the Attorneys General of Ontario and Alberta submit that a more deferential standard is appropriate — one in which an error of law or principle must be found before intervention will be warranted.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue for correctness standard on s. 680(1) review; Crown and AGs argue for deferential standard requiring legal error.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue absence of 'show cause' in s. 680(1) implies less deferential review than trial bail reviews under ss. 520 and 521.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the CLA make two main submissions. First, they point to ss. 520 and 521 of the Code — the bail review provisions that apply at the trial stage. Unlike s. 680(1), those provisions require the applicant to “show cause” to succeed on a bail review. In St-Cloud, this Court observed that the words “show cause” signal a less interventionist, more deferential approach to bail reviews at the trial stage. In doing so, the Court noted the absence of similar language in s. 680(1) (paras. 97-104). Hence, it is argued that s. 680(1) should be interpreted as invoking a less deferential standard than the standard applicable at trial.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 680(1) review is less deferential than trial bail reviews due to absence of 'show cause' language.

propositions.text: Court rejects argument that absence of 'show cause' in s. 680(1) implies less deferential review.
propositions.quote: While the words “show cause” are not found in s. 680(1), I am not convinced that their absence is as significant as Mr. Oland and the CLA suggest.

propositions.text: More explicit language would be expected if Parliament intended panel to substitute opinion without more.
propositions.quote: I would have expected more explicit language than the language used in s. 680(1), if Parliament intended the review to be a process in which the panel could, without more, simply substitute its opinion for that of the judge.

propositions.text: In St-Cloud, Court noted comments on 'show cause' were not determinative of s. 680(1) review type.
propositions.quote: in St-Cloud, at para. 104, Wagner J. for the Court stated that his comments were not determinative of the type of review contemplated by s. 680(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the argument that s. 680(1) review is less deferential due to absence of 'show cause', citing St-Cloud.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland and CLA argue constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c) depends on robust correctness review.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland and the CLA submit that the constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c) hinges on the existence of a robust correctness review.

propositions.text: They rely on Farinacci where Arbour J.A. said correctness standard assesses individual decisions and prevents personal predilections.
propositions.quote: Although its application is often not free from difficulty, and although judges may differ in its application, it is a standard against which the correctness of individual decisions can be assessed. In contrast, a standardless sweep would preclude any debate regarding the correctness of a decision made under its authority as it would authorize judges to pursue their own personal predilections.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Oland and CLA argue s. 679(3)(c) constitutionality depends on robust correctness review, citing Farinacci.

propositions.text: Court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive as it concerned constitutionality not review standard here.
propositions.quote: I do not find this reference to be persuasive. In Farinacci, the Court of Appeal was focused on the constitutionality of s. 679(3)(c), a matter that does not concern us in this appeal.

propositions.text: Correctness is not the only meaningful review form protecting against vagueness; review nature here is unsettled.
propositions.quote: it does not follow that the nature of that review must invoke a correctness standard along the lines suggested by Mr. Oland and the CLA.

propositions.text: In absence of constitutional challenge, no need to decide review standard beyond noting Court of Appeal comments are not dispositive.
propositions.quote: in the absence of a constitutional challenge, I do not consider it necessary to decide this issue beyond concluding that the comments of the Court of Appeal are not dispositive in settling the nature of review contemplated under s. 680(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Farinacci reference unpersuasive and declines to decide review standard absent constitutional challenge.

propositions.text: A panel reviewing a single judge's decision under s. 680(1) should follow three principles regarding deference and intervention.
propositions.quote: a panel reviewing a decision of a single judge under s. 680(1) should be guided by the following three principles

propositions.text: First, absent palpable and overriding error, the review panel must defer to the judge’s findings of fact.
propositions.quote: absent palpable and overriding error, the review panel must show deference to the judge’s findings of fact

propositions.text: Second, the review panel may substitute its decision if the judge erred in law or principle and the error was material to the outcome.
propositions.quote: the review panel may intervene and substitute its decision for that of the judge where it is satisfied that the judge erred in law or in principle, and the error was material to the outcome

propositions.text: Third, absent legal error, the review panel may substitute its decision if the decision was clearly unwarranted.
propositions.quote: in the absence of legal error, the review panel may intervene and substitute its decision for that of the judge where it concludes that the decision was clearly unwarranted

paragraphs.summary: The court states three principles guiding review panels under s. 680(1): defer to fact findings absent palpable error, intervene for material legal errors, and intervene if decision is clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: This approach balances meaningful review with deference and aligns with trial stage review, except for s. 469 offences.
propositions.quote: This approach allows for meaningful review while extending a measure of deference to the judge’s decision. It also achieves symmetry with the review process at the trial stage, save for those offences identified in s. 469 of the Code

propositions.text: Gary T. Trotter explains that endorsing correctness for s. 680 creates differential standards for s. 469 vs. non-469 offences, which is anomalous.
propositions.quote: Focusing on the review of pre-trial bail orders, endorsing a correctness standard in the application of s. 680 creates differential standards of review for s. 469 vs. non-469 offences

propositions.text: There is no principled reason to allow broader review for murder charges under s. 680 than for manslaughter or attempted murder under s. 520.
propositions.quote: There is no principled reason that supports a situation where someone detained on a murder charge enjoys a broader scope of review under s. 680 when compared to a person charged with manslaughter or attempted murder (both non-s. 469 offences) who is dealt with under the narrower s. 520

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the approach balances review and deference, avoiding anomalous differential standards between s. 469 and non-469 offences, citing Gary T. Trotter.

propositions.text: No formal procedure governs the chief justice’s decision to direct a panel review under the Code.
propositions.quote: There is no formal procedure in the Code governing the chief justice’s decision to direct a panel review

propositions.text: Courts of appeal have adopted different approaches and formality levels for the chief justice’s gatekeeping function.
propositions.quote: courts of appeal have adopted different approaches and levels of formality

propositions.text: The procedural aspects of the chief justice’s gatekeeping function are not before the court and will not be addressed.
propositions.quote: The procedural aspects of the gatekeeping function are not before us and I do not propose to address them

propositions.text: Some guidance can be given on the test the chief justice should apply when deciding to direct a panel review.
propositions.quote: Some guidance can, however, be given as to the test a chief justice should apply in deciding whether to direct a panel review

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no formal procedure governs the chief justice’s decision to direct a panel review but offers guidance on the test to apply.

propositions.text: The chief justice should consider directing a review where it is arguable the judge made material errors of fact or law or the decision was clearly unwarranted.
propositions.quote: the chief justice should consider directing a review where it is arguable that the judge committed material errors of fact or law in arriving at the impugned decision, or that the impugned decision was clearly unwarranted in the circumstances

paragraphs.summary: The court states the chief justice should direct a review if it is arguable the judge made material errors or the decision was clearly unwarranted.

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was an ideal candidate for bail aside from the seriousness of his offence.
propositions.quote: By all accounts, aside from the seriousness of the offence for which Mr. Oland was convicted, he presented as an ideal candidate for bail

propositions.text: The appeal judge rightly ignored Mr. Oland’s prominence and any uninformed public opinion about the case.
propositions.quote: The notoriety of this case, which stemmed largely from his prominence in the community, and any uninformed public opinion about it, were rightly ignored by the appeal judge

propositions.text: Mr. Oland was entitled to the same treatment as someone less prominent.
propositions.quote: Mr. Oland, I emphasize, was entitled to the same treatment as someone less prominent

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Oland was an ideal bail candidate and was rightly treated like any less prominent person by the appeal judge.

propositions.text: If Mr. Oland did not qualify for release, no one convicted of similarly serious offences would be released without unique or strong appeal grounds.
propositions.quote: if he did not qualify for release, no one convicted of a similarly serious offence would ever be released, absent a showing of unique or exceptionally strong grounds of appeal

propositions.text: Parliament did not restrict bail pending appeal for persons convicted of murder or other serious crimes and courts should respect this.
propositions.quote: Parliament did not restrict the availability of bail pending appeal for persons convicted of murder or any other serious crime and courts should respect this

propositions.text: For serious offences, where no public safety or flight concerns exist and grounds surpass 'not frivolous', reviewability may outweigh enforceability, allowing release.
propositions.quote: even in the case of very serious offences, where there are no public safety or flight concerns and the grounds of appeal clearly surpass the “not frivolous” criterion, a court may well conclude that the reviewability interest overshadows the enforceability interest such that detention will not be necessary in the public interest

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues no serious offender would be released without strong grounds; the court says Parliament allows bail pending appeal if grounds surpass 'not frivolous' and no safety risk.

propositions.text: Each case requires contextual analysis considering factors like criminal record, public safety, flight risk, and release plan strength.
propositions.quote: a contextual analysis that can account for these differences is required

propositions.text: Factors such as prior record, safety, flight risk, or weak release plans may justify detention in other cases.
propositions.quote: there may be operative factors in other cases, such as a prior criminal record, public safety and flight risk concerns, or a weaker release plan, which could raise concerns warranting detention

paragraphs.summary: The court states bail decisions require contextual analysis of factors like criminal record, safety, flight risk, and release plan strength.

propositions.text: The appeal judge found no appreciable public safety or flight risk concerns and grounds of appeal were clearly arguable.
propositions.quote: the appeal judge was satisfied that there were no appreciable public safety or flight risk concerns and the grounds of appeal were “clearly arguable”

propositions.text: The appeal judge overlooked the trial judge’s finding that Mr. Oland’s crime gravitated more toward manslaughter than first degree murder.
propositions.quote: the appeal judge overlooked what I consider to be an important finding made by the trial judge, namely, that in the circumstances, Mr. Oland’s crime gravitated more toward the offence of manslaughter than to first degree murder

propositions.text: This finding lessened moral blameworthiness, attenuating crime seriousness and enforceability interest.
propositions.quote: This finding was important because it served to lessen Mr. Oland’s degree of moral blameworthiness, thereby attenuating the seriousness of the crime and hence the enforceability interest

propositions.text: These considerations should have tipped the scale in favour of release; detention was clearly unwarranted and the Court of Appeal erred in not intervening.
propositions.quote: the cumulative effect of these considerations ought to have tipped the scale in favour of release. In other words, Mr. Oland’s detention was clearly unwarranted and the Court of Appeal erred in failing to intervene

paragraphs.summary: The appeal judge found no safety risk and clearly arguable grounds; the court finds he overlooked manslaughter finding, which lessened seriousness, so detention was unwarranted and appeal court erred.

propositions.text: The appeal judge erred by requiring more than 'clearly arguable' grounds, seeking unique circumstances assuring new trial or acquittal.
propositions.quote: he did not apply the correct test in assessing the strength of Mr. Oland’s appeal and the implications flowing from it

propositions.text: The appeal judge required unique circumstances that would virtually assure a new trial or acquittal to justify release.
propositions.quote: none fall in the category of the unique circumstances that would virtually assure a new trial or an acquittal

propositions.text: The appeal judge concluded release would undermine public confidence in criminal justice administration.
propositions.quote: the confidence of the reasonable member of the public in the administration of criminal justice would be undermined

propositions.text: Respectfully, the court finds the appeal judge erred; 'clearly arguable' grounds suffice to surpass 'not frivolous' criterion.
propositions.quote: That Mr. Oland’s grounds were “clearly arguable” was enough to establish that they clearly surpassed the “not frivolous” criterion

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appeal judge erred by requiring unique circumstances beyond 'clearly arguable' grounds, which suffice to surpass 'not frivolous'.

propositions.text: Had the appeal not been moot, the court would have set aside detention and ordered release pending appeal.
propositions.quote: I would have set aside Mr. Oland’s detention order and ordered his release pending appeal

propositions.text: Because the appeal is moot, the court allows the appeal but makes no further order.
propositions.quote: because the appeal is moot, I would simply allow the appeal and make no further order. Appeal allowed

paragraphs.summary: The court would have ordered release pending appeal but allows the moot appeal with no further order.
